PURPOSE. The page computes arccot 5 = arctan(1/5) to 63 decimal places. The heading is 'Circuli Quadratura nova' (a new quadrature of the circle). The next page computes arccot 70 in the same way. The combination arccot 5 and arccot 70 (presumably with arccot 99 on a later page) points to the Machin-type formula pi/4 = 4 arctan(1/5) - arctan(1/70) + arctan(1/99). That formula is known from Euler and was used by Rutherford in 1841. The page itself states no formula for pi.

HEADING. 'I. Acotg.5 = (1) - (3)'. My reading: arccot 5 = [sum of the positive terms, beginning with term (1)] - [sum of the negative terms, beginning with term (3)]. This is exactly the layout of the page.

SERIES. arccot 5 = sum_{k>=0} (-1)^k / ((2k+1) 5^(2k+1)).
Write T_n = 1/(n 5^n). The key device is 1/5^n = 2^n/10^n, so T_n = (2^n/n) * 10^(-n). Each term is therefore a single exact division of a power of 2 by n, then shifted by n decimal places. All numbers are written as 63 decimals, in groups of 10 digits.

results.what: arctan(1/5) computed to 63 decimals by the Gregory series. It uses 1/5^n = 2^n/10^n and groups terms whose denominators give compatible repeating periods, so the repeating decimals are added exactly. The result is correct to 62 places.
results.modern_name: Gregory-Leibniz arctangent series; Machin-type high-precision evaluation of arctan(1/5)
results.usually_credited_to: Gregory (1671), Machin (1706); arctan(1/5) evaluations by Machin, Euler and Vega (18th century)

results.what: Apparent plan: the heading 'Circuli Quadratura nova' plus arccot 5 here and arccot 70 on the next page suggest the pi formula pi/4 = 4 arccot 5 - arccot 70 + arccot 99, or a related combination.
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (18th c.); used by Rutherford (1841) for 208 digits of pi

deep.surprise_reason: This is a careful but entirely standard 18th/19th-century high-precision computation of arctan(1/5) to about 63 places. Gauss's interest in arctangent formulas for pi, and in decomposing arctangents via factorization of n^2+1, is well documented (e.g. his formula 12 arctan(1/18) + 8 arctan(1/57) - 5 arctan(1/239)). The grouping-by-period trick is a clever bookkeeping device, not new mathematics.
